tips.title: Arterioles widen; capillaries do nothing
tips.body: *The capillaries dilate* and *the capillaries move to the surface* are both wrong, and both are common. A capillary wall is one cell thick with no muscle. Say: **the arterioles widen, so more blood flows near the surface**.

tips.title: It is the evaporation that cools
tips.body: Sweat sitting on the skin does nothing. **Evaporation** takes energy from the skin, which is why sweating works poorly in humid air. An answer that says *sweat cools you* has described rather than explained.

tips.title: Denatured, never killed
tips.body: An enzyme is a protein and was never alive. Heat breaks the bonds holding its shape, so the **active site changes shape** and the substrate no longer fits. That wording is what the mark is for.

tips.title: Shivering is the odd one out
tips.body: Every other response changes the **rate** at which heat is lost. Shivering is the only one that **generates** heat, through increased respiration in the muscles. If a question asks which response produces heat, that is the answer.

tips.title: Cold is reversible, hot is not
tips.body: Too cold merely **slows** enzymes, and warming fixes it. Too hot **denatures** them permanently. That asymmetry is the answer to *why is a high temperature more dangerous*, and it is worth one clean sentence.

steps.title: Why temperature must be controlled
steps.body:
Human body temperature is held at about **37 °C**, and the reason is **enzymes**.

Every reaction in a cell is controlled by an enzyme, and an enzyme works by its **active site** fitting the substrate. Temperature affects that fit in two opposite ways:

- **Too cold.** The molecules move more slowly, so there are fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate. Reactions become **too slow** to keep the body working. This is **reversible** — warm it up again and the enzyme works as before.
- **Too hot.** The enzyme **denatures**: the bonds holding its shape break, the **active site changes shape**, and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme stops working, and this is **not reversible**.

That asymmetry matters. Being cold slows you down; being too hot damages you permanently. It is why a high fever is dangerous in a way that being chilly is not, and it is why the word **denatured** — not *killed* — is the one to use.

Controlling temperature is therefore part of **homeostasis**: keeping conditions inside the body constant so that cells can work, whatever is happening outside.

steps.title: The skin, and who is in charge
steps.body:
Thermoregulation involves the **skin** as the effector and the **hypothalamus** as the control centre. The specification names three parts, and each has a distinct job.

**The hypothalamus** — in the brain. It contains receptors that **monitor the temperature of the blood** flowing through it, and it receives information from temperature receptors in the skin. It then **coordinates the response**, sending impulses to the skin and muscles. It is the **thermoregulatory centre**.

**The epidermis** — the **outer** layer of the skin. It is a **protective** layer: it forms a barrier against water loss and against pathogens entering. It contains no blood vessels.

**The dermis** — the **thicker inner** layer, and where almost everything happens. It contains:

- **sweat glands**, which produce sweat
- **blood vessels**, which widen or narrow
- **hair erector muscles**, which raise or lower the hairs
- **receptors**, which detect the temperature of the surroundings
- a layer of **fat** below it, which insulates

So if a question asks which layer does the work, the answer is the **dermis**. The epidermis protects; the dermis responds.

steps.title: Vasodilation, said precisely
steps.body:
This is where most marks in the topic are lost, so it is worth being exact.

**The blood vessels that change are the arterioles** — the small arteries that supply the skin capillaries. They have muscle in their walls, so they can widen and narrow.

**The capillaries themselves do not change.** They have walls one cell thick with no muscle, so they cannot dilate or constrict. And they certainly do not **move** — a capillary is fixed in the tissue.

So three common phrasings are wrong:

- *The capillaries dilate* — they cannot.
- *The capillaries move closer to the surface* — they do not move at all.
- *The blood vessels move up and down* — nothing moves.

The correct version is one sentence: **the arterioles widen, so more blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, and more heat is lost.**

**What is actually being changed** is the **amount of blood** flowing through the vessels near the surface, not their position. Widening the supply increases the flow; narrowing it reduces the flow.

One more piece of precision: vasodilation **does not cool the blood**. It increases the **rate at which heat is lost** from the skin to the surroundings — which is why it works less well on a very hot day, when the surroundings are nearly as warm as you are.

steps.title: Going deeper: the same loop, a third time
steps.body:
**The pattern you have now seen three times.** Thyroxine, blood glucose and temperature are all controlled the same way:

1. A **receptor** detects a change — here, receptors in the **hypothalamus** monitoring blood temperature, and receptors in the **dermis** detecting the surroundings.
2. A **coordination centre** processes it — the **hypothalamus**.
3. **Effectors** respond — the **blood vessels**, **sweat glands**, **hair erector muscles** and **skeletal muscles**.
4. The response **opposes** the change.
5. As the temperature returns to normal, the response **switches off**.

Writing the answer in that shape earns marks even where you are unsure of a detail, because it shows you understand it as a control system.

**Why there are several responses rather than one.** Each one is limited. Sweating fails in humid air, because sweat cannot evaporate into air that is already saturated — which is why a humid 30 °C feels far worse than a dry 30 °C. Vasodilation fails when the surroundings are as warm as the skin, because heat only flows from hot to cold. Having several mechanisms means the body is not defeated when one of them stops working.

**Shivering is the odd one out, and it is worth noticing why.** Every other response **conserves** heat or **loses** it — it changes the rate at which heat moves. Shivering is the only one that **generates** heat, by increasing respiration. That is also why it is the response of last resort: it costs energy, whereas narrowing a blood vessel is free.

**Three phrasings that cost marks.**

- *The capillaries dilate* or *move to the surface* — no. The **arterioles widen**; the capillaries do nothing.
- *Sweat cools you* — only its **evaporation** does.
- *Enzymes are killed* — they are **denatured**. An enzyme was never alive, and the examiner is testing whether you know what denaturing is.

**And one about hairs.** In humans, hairs standing up traps very little air — it is largely a vestigial response, which is why we get goosebumps rather than genuine insulation. You should still name it, because the specification does, but it explains why shivering matters more to us than it does to a furry animal.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Body temperature is held at about **37 °C** so that **enzymes** work.
- **Too cold**: reactions are **too slow**, and it is **reversible**. **Too hot**: enzymes **denature**, and it is **not**.
- The **hypothalamus** monitors the temperature of the **blood** and coordinates the response.
- The **epidermis** is the outer, **protective** layer. The **dermis** holds the sweat glands, blood vessels, hair erector muscles and receptors.
- **Too hot**: **vasodilation** — the **arterioles widen**, so more blood flows near the surface and **more heat is lost**.
- **Sweating**: sweat **evaporates**, and evaporation **takes energy from the skin**.
- **Hairs lie flat**, trapping less air.
- **Too cold**: **vasoconstriction** — the **arterioles narrow**, so **less heat is lost**.
- **Shivering**: muscles contract rapidly, increasing **respiration**, which **releases energy as heat**. It is the only response that **generates** heat.
- **Hairs stand up**, trapping air as insulation, and **sweating stops**.
- The **capillaries do not dilate or move** — only the **arterioles** change.
- Say **denatured**, not killed; and say the **evaporation** cools, not the sweat.
- Several mechanisms exist because each one fails under some conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain how the body responds when its temperature rises above normal, naming the part of the brain involved and describing three responses.
questions.solution: The hypothalamus, which is part of the brain, contains receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through it, and it also receives information from temperature receptors in the dermis of the skin. When it detects that the body temperature has risen above normal it coordinates a response. First, vasodilation occurs: the arterioles that supply the capillaries near the surface of the skin widen, so that more blood flows through those capillaries and more heat is lost from the skin to the surroundings. It is important to note that the capillaries themselves do not widen or move, because their walls are only one cell thick and contain no muscle. Second, the sweat glands in the dermis release sweat on to the surface of the skin. The sweat then evaporates, and evaporation takes energy from the skin, which cools it. Third, the hair erector muscles relax so that the hairs lie flat, trapping less air and therefore providing less insulation. Together these responses reduce the body temperature back towards thirty seven degrees Celsius, and as it returns to normal the responses are switched off, which makes this an example of negative feedback.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Detection.** The **hypothalamus** contains receptors monitoring the temperature of the **blood**, and receives information from receptors in the **dermis**. It coordinates the response.

**Response 1 — vasodilation.** The **arterioles** supplying the skin capillaries **widen**, so **more blood flows** through the capillaries near the surface and **more heat is lost** to the surroundings.

Say *arterioles*. The capillaries do not widen — their walls are one cell thick with no muscle — and they do not move.

**Response 2 — sweating.** The **sweat glands** in the **dermis** release sweat on to the skin. The sweat **evaporates**, and **evaporation takes energy from the skin**, cooling it.

The cooling is the evaporation, not the sweat.

**Response 3 — hairs lie flat.** The erector muscles **relax**, so **less air is trapped** and there is less insulation.

**The result.** Temperature falls back towards **37 °C**, and as it does the responses switch off — negative feedback, the same shape as thyroxine and blood glucose.

questions.prompt: Explain why the human body must keep its internal temperature close to 37 °C, referring to enzymes, and explain why a high temperature is more dangerous than a low one.
questions.solution: Every chemical reaction that takes place in a cell is controlled by an enzyme, and an enzyme works because its active site has a shape that fits the substrate. If the body temperature falls too low, the molecules move more slowly and there are fewer collisions between the enzyme and the substrate, so the reactions in cells become too slow to keep the body functioning properly. This effect is reversible, because warming the body up again restores the normal rate of reaction. If the body temperature rises too high, the bonds that hold the enzyme in its shape break and the enzyme becomes denatured, which means that its active site changes shape so that the substrate no longer fits into it. The enzyme then stops working altogether, and this change cannot be reversed by cooling the body down again. A high temperature is therefore more dangerous than a low one, because the damage it does to enzymes is permanent while the effect of being too cold is not.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why enzymes matter.** Every reaction in a cell is controlled by an **enzyme**, and an enzyme works because its **active site** fits the substrate.

**Too cold.** Molecules move more **slowly**, so there are **fewer collisions** between enzyme and substrate. Reactions become **too slow** to keep the body working.

This is **reversible**: warming the body restores the normal rate.

**Too hot.** The bonds holding the enzyme's shape **break**, so the enzyme is **denatured** — the **active site changes shape** and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme stops working.

This is **not reversible**: cooling down does not restore the shape.

**The conclusion.** A high temperature is more dangerous because the damage is **permanent**, while being too cold only slows things down temporarily.

Use the word **denatured**, not *killed*. An enzyme is a protein and was never alive, and the examiner is checking that you know what denaturing actually is.

examTechnique.body:
Start with the hypothalamus detecting the change, then give the responses, then say the temperature returns to normal.

Name the arterioles when describing vasodilation or vasoconstriction, and say what happens to the blood flow rather than to the position of any vessel.

For sweating, say that the sweat evaporates and that evaporation takes energy from the skin.

For shivering, name respiration as the source of the heat.

Use the word denatured about enzymes, and say that the active site changes shape.

If the question asks for three responses, give three: the blood vessels, the sweat glands and the hairs, and add shivering when the body is cold.
examinerErrors: Saying the capillaries dilate or constrict.
Saying blood vessels move closer to or further from the surface.
Saying sweat cools the body without mentioning evaporation.
Saying enzymes are killed rather than denatured.
Saying shivering moves warm blood around rather than releasing heat by respiration.
Giving the epidermis as the layer containing the sweat glands.
Leaving out the hypothalamus when asked how the response is coordinated.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer recognises this as the third example of the same control loop and writes it in that shape: receptor, coordination centre, effector, opposing response, switch-off. It is exact about the arterioles and never has a capillary moving or dilating. It attributes the cooling to **evaporation** and can then explain why humidity defeats it. It notices that shivering is the only response that generates heat rather than redirecting it, and it uses *denatured* precisely, saying what happens to the active site rather than merely naming the word.
